title: I spent hours trying to build an automated options agent or any agent for stock market and it kept undoing its own fixes and the app is called public
author: skt-yasuo

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the "one order per run" rule shouldn't live in the agent at all. an LLM that re-reads the whole strategy on every edit treats each rule as text it can renegotiate, so it "fixes" one thing and quietly breaks another. put that rule, the premium cap and the spread check in plain code that runs before any order leaves: count orders this run, refuse the second. the agent proposes, the code says yes or no.

also check the scanner ever qualifies. a 0.15-0.30 delta SPY option with 7-21 days left costs far more than ten cents, so that combo may never fire, and an agent told to make it work will start bending rules until it does.

I built Quantradin on that same split: the agent suggests, the desk holds limits it can't edit, all on paper. worth a look at quantradin.com before this goes near a live account.

replies.author: skt-yasuo
replies.body:
This is actually close to what I was starting to suspect. My biggest issue wasn’t that the agent refused to trade — I’m perfectly fine with it returning no trade if nothing qualifies. The problem was that while trying to build the workflow, it repeatedly changed rules I specifically told it to preserve, fixed one issue while reintroducing an older one, and sometimes generated contradictory logic.  
I agree that the critical constraints probably need to sit outside the LLM as immutable checks. The AI can scan and propose a contract, but something deterministic should enforce one-order-per-run, position limits, buying power, premium cap, spread limits, and cooldown before an order can actually go through.  
And yeah, I’m also realizing the $0.10 premium requirement may simply make the scanner return nothing most of the time. I’d rather discover that through testing than have the agent silently change the rules to force a trade.  
Thanks for pointing that out, especially the part about separating the agent’s decision-making from hard-coded execution rules. That actually gives me a much better way to think about how this should be built.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
That's the right conclusion. A few practical things that will make the deterministic layer easier to trust. Keep the rules in a versioned config file (YAML or JSON) that the code reads, and never let the agent edit it, so a change shows up as a diff you can review. Write unit tests for the gate itself, for example by simulating a second order in the same run and checking that it gets refused, and rerun them whenever anything changes. Then have every scan log why it returned no trade (which condition failed), so silence never looks like a bug.

For the $0.10 premium problem, run the scanner over a few weeks of history or live data in dry-run mode with no orders, and count how often anything qualifies. If it's nearly never, you can loosen one rule at a time on purpose and see what changes, instead of the agent bending rules to force a trade.

Short-dated index options also get wide spreads and gappy quotes around scheduled releases like CPI, FOMC and major earnings, so a "no entries within N minutes of a release" rule is cheap to add. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing that you could use for it, or any clean calendar.

And paper trade it for a while before it gets anywhere near a live account.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
that drift is the worst part, it fixes one thing and quietly rewrites a rule from three messages back. keeping the rules in a file it can't edit fixed most of it for me.

part of why I built Quantradin too: the strategy runs on paper as written and every trade is logged, so you can check it did what you said. free, quantradin.com
